research.abstract: Abstract Background Rickettsia akari , the causative agent of rickettsialpox, is an obligate intracellular pathogen with a highly reduced genome encoding numerous hypothetical proteins (HPs) of unknown function. Many of these HPs are expressed during host-cell infection, yet their roles in bacterial physiology and potential contribution to virulence remain unclear. Methodology/Principal Findings We performed an integrative in silico characterization of 54 R. akari HPs previously identified by mass spectrometry in purified bacterial cells. Using a benchmarked computational workflow, we predicted their physicochemical properties, subcellular localization, putative secretion signals, protein folds, potential interaction partners, and evolutionary conservation. Most HPs were predicted to be thermostable. The majority of HPs were predicted to be cytoplasmic (37.00%) or membrane-associated (29.63%). Predicted features associated with the type IV secretion system were more frequent than those associated with type I secretion. Network and structural analyses identified candidate HPs with features consistent with potential roles in outer membrane assembly, host-cell interaction, and immune modulation, including predicted peptidyl-prolyl cis/trans isomerases, oxidoreductases, methyltransferases, and putative E3 ubiquitin ligases. Several HPs were predicted to be antigenic and showed conservation across multiple rickettsial genomes. Molecular docking and normal mode analysis supported the plausibility of selected predicted protein-protein and protein-ligand interactions. Evolutionary analyses indicated predominant purifying selection among the analyzed HPs. A8GP20 showed elevated sequence divergence and warrants further investigation as a potential effector candidate. Conclusions/Significance Our findings prioritize A8GPG8, A8GP63, A8GNV4, A8GMM8, A8GM41, A8GMJ7, A8GMI5, A8GP20, A8GN23, A8GMB4, A8GM08, and A8GM39 as promising candidates for experimental validation of their predicted functions and potential roles in R. akari biology and pathogenicity. This work provides an integrative and reproducible bioinformatic framework to guide functional discovery in R. akari and related neglected intracellular pathogens, and identifies candidate proteins for future studies of rickettsial pathogenesis, antigen discovery, and therapeutic target development. Author summary Rickettsialpox is a neglected febrile illness caused by the bacterium Rickettsia akari and transmitted by mouse mites. Although R. akari has a small genome, many of its proteins remain uncharacterized and are annotated as “hypothetical proteins”. These proteins may contribute to the bacterium’s ability to infect host cells and cause disease, but their functions are poorly understood. We used an integrative computational approach to characterize 54 uncharacterized proteins previously identified in R. akari cells by mass spectrometry. Our analyses suggest that many of these proteins are predicted to be stable and associated with the bacterial membrane, whereas several may interact with host cells, potentially through a bacterial secretion system. We identified promising candidates that may contribute to host-cell interactions, immune modulation, outer membrane assembly, and other processes important for bacterial survival. Several proteins were predicted to be antigenic and showed conservation across multiple rickettsial genomes, suggesting potential value for future diagnostic or vaccine studies. By prioritizing the most promising uncharacterized proteins for experimental validation, our study provides new insights into the biology and pathogenicity of R. akari and offers a framework for studying similar proteins in other neglected intracellular pathogens.

research.abstract: ABSTRACT Island radiations provide ideal frameworks for studying the molecular basis of convergent evolution. The rapid diversification of Dysdera spiders in Canary Islands provides a striking example, with repeated dietary shifts towards specialisation on woodlice, accompanied by morphological, metabolic, and behavioural modifications that facilitate the exploitation of this heavy-metal-rich prey. Here, we investigate two independent events of dietary specialisation on different islands. By analysing six high-quality genome-assemblies, including three newly generated in this study, we investigate the genomic signals of positive selection and relaxed selection in protein-coding genes, upstream regulatory regions, and gene family turnover rates. We detected signatures of positive selection associated with the two specialists, accompanied by a twofold increase in gene loss rates relative to generalist ancestors. Notably, positive selection targeted a smaller, functionally coherent set of genes, potentially involved in detoxification likely through heavy metal excretion. In contrast, relaxation of selection affected a broader set of genes associated with functions that may have become dispensable under the new dietary regime. Furthermore, we found contractions in gene families associated with vesicular transport, potentially reflecting a reduced reliance on vesicle-mediated metal accumulation. Overall, our findings suggest that similar ecological pressures can drive parallel, yet non-identical, adaptive and non-adaptive responses, pointing to partially predictable evolutionary trajectories in an island radiation.

research.abstract: Time from symptom onset to first care may be a modifiable determinant of COVID-19 outcomes, but it is rarely quantified in primary care. This retrospective cohort study included all 5,248 confirmed SARS-CoV-2 cases (RT-PCR or certified rapid antigen test) notified to the national surveillance system (SINOLAVE) by a large family medicine unit of the Mexican Social Security Institute (IMSS) in Leon, Mexico, between April 2020 and April 2021. Pandemic waves were classified using the official IMSS definition. Wave profiles were compared with chi-square tests and Bonferroni correction, and predictors of death were assessed by multivariable logistic regression, with sensitivity analyses adjusting for severity signs at first contact. Of the cases, 53.8% were female, mean age was 41.1 years, and 317 deaths (6.0%) were registered. Median time to first care was 3 days (interquartile range: 2-5). Case fatality was 3.0% among patients presenting within 3 days and 9.1% among those presenting later. Later presentation (> 3 days) was associated with death (adjusted odds ratio = 1.98; 95% confidence interval: 1.47-2.65), but the association was attenuated after adjustment for severity signs at first contact (adjusted odds ratio = 1.20; 95% confidence interval: 0.85-1.69), which were more frequent among later presenters (21.8% vs. 9.3%). From the first to the second wave, fever (76.1% to 56.9%), diabetes (22.8% to 9.6%), and case fatality (10.5% to 4.8%) decreased, whereas anosmia and dysgeusia increased (all p < 0.001). Surveillance data cannot distinguish clinical progression during delay from late presentation of already severe patients. Delay persisted despite universal entitlement to care, indicating that insurance coverage alone did not ensure timely presentation; prospective cohorts measuring severity at onset are needed.

research.abstract: Abstract Diabetic retinopathy is a leading cause of preventable blindness. Because it is asymptomatic until substantial damage has occurred, periodic retinal examination is essential for early detection. Evidence on uptake where eye services are co-located with diabetes care in Ethiopia is lacking. This study assessed the prevalence of, and factors associated with, adequate diabetic retinopathy screening practice among adults with diabetes attending Menelik II Comprehensive Specialized Hospital, Addis Ababa. We conducted an institution-based cross-sectional study from December 2023 to February 2024 among adults with type 1 or type 2 diabetes on follow-up for at least three months, selected by systematic random sampling and interviewed with a structured questionnaire. Knowledge and attitude were classified using a modified Bloom’s cut-off of 80%, and screening practice as adequate when at least two of three recommended practices were met. Factors associated with adequate practice were identified using multivariable logistic regression. Of 404 patients approached, 371 were interviewed and included in the analysis (response rate 91.8%). Adequate screening practice was found in 139 participants (37.5%, 95% confidence interval [CI] 32.7–42.5); 62.0% had adequate knowledge and 72.8% a favorable attitude. Adequate practice was associated with adequate knowledge (adjusted odds ratio [AOR] 5.10, 95% CI 2.81– 9.25), a known eye disorder (AOR 3.96, 95% CI 2.11–7.43), higher education (AOR 3.82, 95% CI 1.33–10.95), age 41–65 years (AOR 3.15, 95% CI 1.10–9.03) and being married (AOR 1.73, 95% CI 1.01–2.97). Cost, lack of time and travel distance were the most commonly reported barriers. Fewer than four in ten adults with diabetes underwent retinal examination at the recommended frequency despite on-site specialist eye care. The strong association with existing eye disorders suggests that examination is often prompted by ocular problems rather than undertaken for prevention. Strengthening patient education during diabetes follow-up and a direct referral pathway to on-site eye services may improve uptake.

research.abstract: Abstract Background Measles outbreaks are increasing in frequency globally as vaccine coverage decreases. During the 2025-26 Utah-Arizona border outbreak, identifying where and between whom transmission occurred was essential for directing control measures. However, epidemiological data alone are not sufficient to infer transmission patterns. Methods As part of the local and state-wide outbreak investigation, we conducted amplicon-based whole genome sequencing on residual diagnostic samples from confirmed measles cases collected from June 15, 2025–April 30, 2026. We reconstructed viral dispersal across Utah using Bayesian phylogeographic analyses. We evaluated genetic distance thresholds for identifying recent transmission by comparing single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP)-based genetic clusters with known epidemiologic linkages. We then assessed pairwise exposures associated with genetically supported transmission linkage using logistic regression, accounting for network and spatial dependence between pairs. Findings We generated 509 high-quality whole measles virus genomes from 913 patients. In 2025, most viral dispersal events (67.9%) originated in Southwest Utah and Mohave County, Arizona, where the first cases were reported. By 2026, most viral spread (60.5%) occurred outside of this area. A threshold of 0 SNPs identified epidemiologically linked pairs of individuals with a sensitivity of 77.4% and specificity of 92.3%. Household membership (odds ratio (OR): 219.10, 95% credible interval (CI): 112.66-325.53), participation in the same sport (OR: 15.19, 95% CI: 9.75-20.63), and attendance at the same school (OR: 51.5, 95% CI: 36.38-66.61) were independently associated with transmission linkage. Increasing distance between households was associated with reduced odds of linkage (OR: 0.46: 95% CI 0.44-0.48). Interpretation Repeated introductions of measles virus from southwestern Utah seeded transmission elsewhere in Utah, with household, school, and sports exposures contributing to onward transmission. Validated genome-based linkage measures can complement contact tracing by helping public health teams identify likely transmission networks and prioritize investigation when resources are constrained. Funding Epidemiology and Laboratory Capacity (ELC) program at the CDC Research in Context Evidence before this study We searched PubMed and medRxiv as of October 6, 2026 for studies about measles genomic or molecular epidemiology, measles virus transmission modelling, and application of whole genome sequencing of measles virus. English language search terms included “measles”, “measles virus”, “phylodynamic”, “genomic epidemiology”, “molecular epidemiology”, “transmission modelling”, “transmission dynamics”, “sequencing”, “whole genome sequencing”, and “WGS”. Previous studies have primarily utilized N450 sequencing in their outbreak assessments, including phylogenetic and phylogeographic analyses. More recent studies have utilized whole genome sequencing to perform phylogenetic analysis and have overlaid some epidemiological data to assess transmission. To our knowledge, no studies have combined epidemiological and whole genome sequencing data to quantitatively assess drivers of transmission. Added value of this study We integrate detailed epidemiological data with whole genome sequencing, providing a comprehensive analysis of geographic spread and key drivers of transmission in the Utah-Arizona border outbreak. We generated whole genome sequences for 56% of confirmed cases, high sequence coverage that enabled us to identify an appropriate genomic threshold and approximate direct transmission links. Our findings illustrate a change in geographic transmission as the outbreak persisted and highlighted household, school, and sports based transmission as primary sources of exposure. Implications of all the available evidence Our findings demonstrate the utility of measles surveillance using whole genome sequencing paired with epidemiological data. As measles outbreaks increase in frequency, new approaches are needed to characterize the key drivers of transmission. By integrating epidemiologic and genomic data, we identified genomic thresholds for transmission that can be applied in settings where extensive epidemiologic data are unavailable. Ultimately, utilizing genomic and epidemiological data together will strengthen our surveillance of future measles outbreaks.

research.abstract: Estimating the effective sample size (ESS) is fundamental in Bayesian phylogenetic inference to account for autocorrelation in MCMC samples. While methods for continuous parameters are well established, the discrete and high-dimensional nature of treespace poses substantial challenges. In this paper, we introduce a new approach based on Conditional Clade Distributions (CCDs) to emulate MCMC chains with known ESS bounds. We compare existing tree ESS estimators with novel approaches that utilize CCDs as tractable tree distributions, as well as a new probabilistic estimator based on differences in clade frequencies between independent chains. Using our emulated chains from both simulated and real datasets, we assess estimators for their ability to recover the true ESS (accuracy), their insensitivity to the removal of autocorrelated samples from the chain (stability), and their tolerance to combining multiple chains together (robustness). We further examine how multimodality and poor inter-mode chain mixing can compromise the reliability of tree ESS estimates. These findings indicate that our new CCD-based estimators perform comparably to existing approaches with respect to accuracy, stability, and robustness. In contrast, the probabilistic estimator and two previously recommended methods incur prohibitive computational costs for long chains. Together, these results establish a new framework for evaluating tree ESS estimators using CCD-based emulated MCMC chains and demonstrate their performance and current limitations in practical phylogenetic analyses. The expanded suite of tree ESS estimators is available in the user-friendly TreeStat2 software package for BEAST 2.

research.abstract: Abstract Background Chronic inflammation persists in populations with high HIV and tuberculosis (TB) burden, even during suppressive therapy. Tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) is a key mediator, but its correlates beyond infectious status remain unclear in people living with HIV on stable antiretroviral therapy and who are virologically suppressed. We investigated clinical, metabolic, and neurohormonal correlates of TNF-α in a Zambian cohort. Methods This was a cross-sectional study, which included 227 adults recruited from the outpatient medical clinic at Livingstone University Teaching Hospital in the Southern Province of Zambia. Simple and multivariable linear regression analyses were performed to determine independent associations with plasma TNF-α levels. Models were adjusted for HIV serostatus and history of TB. Standardized beta coefficients (β_std) were computed to compare the relative magnitude of associations across predictors measured on different scales. Results Among 227 participants, 64.8% were living with HIV (95.3% on integrase strand transfer inhibitor-based ART) and 14.0% had a history of tuberculosis. In multivariable analysis, the strongest independent associations with TNF-α were observed within the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS): angiotensin II (β = 1.18 per pg/mL, p < 0.001; β_std = 0.51) and aldosterone (β = 0.884 per pg/mL, p < 0.001; β_std = 0.47). Living with HIV serostatus was also independently associated with higher TNF-α (β = 2581.1 pg/mL, p = 0.018; β_std = 0.19), while the history of TB was not. Significant metabolic factors associated with TNF-α levels included VLDL (β = 4397.4 per mmol/L, p = 0.038; β_std = 0.16) and triglycerides (β = 1971.6 per mmol/L, p = 0.034; β_std = 0.17). Inflammatory markers sST2 (β = 104.4 per ng/mL, p < 0.001; β_std = 0.31), IL-17 A (β = 1.137 per pg/mL, p = 0.003; β_std = 0.21), and D-dimer (β = 0.037 per pg/mL, p = 0.001; β_std = 0.22) were independently associated, as was plasma potassium (β = 107.3 per mmol/L, p < 0.001; β_std = 0.46). Renin, IL-6, IL-5, hs-CRP, and left ventricular mass were not associated with TNF-α. Conclusion In this high-burden population, RAAS activation was an independent correlate of TNF-α, exceeding the effect of HIV serostatus. These findings support the hypothesis that RAAS inhibition may have anti-inflammatory effects; however, this remains to be tested in prospective and interventional studies.

research.abstract: Abstract Eukaryotic genomes exhibit astounding levels of complexity. Much of this complexity resides in repetitive DNA thought to evolve neutrally, meaning that its impact on fitness is so small that natural selection cannot act efficiently to favor or purge it. Yet, repetitive DNA greatly facilitates the generation of structural variants (SVs), which fuel evolution with both adaptive and deleterious genetic variation. How SVs involving initially neutral repetitive DNA can bring new evolutionarily meaningful impacts is not well understood, in part because finding and interpreting molecular signatures of these transitions using comparative genomics over long evolutionary timescales is challenging. Here, we document one such transition over a microevolutionary timescale using budding yeast population genomics. We characterize multiple massive amplifications of the Y’ element, a highly polymorphic and dispensable subtelomeric tandem repeat. We uncover extreme structural diversity in Y’ tandem amplifications among near-isogenic strains and show that these amplifications bring a significant fitness cost. We further link Y’ amplifications with transcriptome rewiring, heightened DNA replication stress sensitivity, and DNA damage response activation. Together, our results support a model by which massive subtelomeric tandem amplification pushed a repetitive DNA family outside of effective neutrality to become deleterious. Significance Statement Extant eukaryotic genomes harbor vast amounts of repetitive DNA elements hypothesized to be non-functional and to have accumulated and persisted through neutral evolutionary processes without substantially affecting organismal fitness. Here, we report that an entire non-functional DNA family evolved out of effective neutrality in the baker’s yeast S. cerevisiae . The Y′ elements, a family of non-functional subtelomeric repeats, have repeatedly undergone dramatic tandem amplifications at chromosome ends across independently evolving S. cerevisiae populations. We show that these amplifications confer fitness defects of sufficient magnitude to be considered non-neutral within the population-genetic environment of the species. These amplifications are associated with numerous cellular phenotypes that likely contribute to this fitness cost, including core transcriptome rewiring, heightened sensitivity to DNA replication stress and increased DNA damage.

research.abstract: BACKGROUND: Bedaquiline (BDQ), pretomanid (Pa) and linezolid (LZD)-based (BPaL) regimens have transformed rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis (RR-TB) treatment. However, resistance to these drugs is increasingly reported, while longitudinal data integrating clinical, phenotypic and genomic evolution remain limited. CASE PRESENTATION: We report a fatal case of recurrent RR-TB in a 40-year-old South African woman with HIV infection who received BPaL therapy. Following treatment completion, recurrent disease was complicated by pregnancy, treatment interruption and loss to follow-up. She subsequently re-presented with advanced cavitary pulmonary tuberculosis and respiratory failure. Despite re-initiation of BPaL, she deteriorated and died from septic shock. Routine drug susceptibility testing, available posthumously, confirmed resistance to BDQ, Pa and LZD. Seven sequential Mycobacterium tuberculosis isolates collected during treatment underwent minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) testing and whole-genome sequencing. All demonstrated phenotypic resistance to the three BPaL drugs. Serial genomic analysis identified progressive Rv0678 diversification associated with a two-fold increase in BDQ MIC, while resistance-associated rrl and fbiC mutations remained comparatively stable despite persistently elevated LZD and Pa MICs. CONCLUSIONS: This case demonstrates the interaction of treatment interruption, delayed resistance detection and continued within-host bacterial adaptation during BPaL therapy. Longitudinal phenotypic and genomic findings revealed distinct resistance trajectories among BPaL drugs, highlighting the importance of treatment retention, timely susceptibility testing and genomic surveillance for preserving BPaL effectiveness.

research.abstract: Abstract Nishikigoi, ornamental cultivars of the common carp ( Cyprinus carpio ), are economically valuable aquaculture teleosts in which mature females command significantly higher market prices due to superior body conformation and coloration. Consequently, early and non-invasive sex identification is highly desirable for commercial breeding. Although sex determination in common carp follows an XX/XY system, sex-chromosome-specific markers and field-applicable diagnostic methods for Nishikigoi have remained limited. Validation across multiple Nishikigoi varieties and wild common carp demonstrated that primary primer pairs achieved high diagnostic accuracy. research.abstract: Abstract Background The HIV reservoir persists in long-living immune cells after antiretroviral therapy initiation. Proviral DNA integrates at preferential host DNA sites, while HIV transcription continues under treatment, with potential biological consequences. Treated people with HIV remain at increased risk for premature aging and non-AIDS comorbidities compared to people without HIV. Whether HIV reservoir size and activity impact health outcomes during treatment remains unclear. Methods We analyzed 1895 people with HIV using antiretroviral therapy from the 2000HIV cohort to study associations between the reservoir and historic and prospective virologic and immunological response markers, comorbidity outcomes and biological aging scores. The reservoir was assessed by quantifying total and intact proviral HIV DNA in circulating CD4+ T cells, along with measures of HIV transcriptional activity, including cell-associated HIV RNA. Results HIV reservoir markers were highly correlating and associated with older aging scores and adverse virologic outcomes, including quantifiable and residual viremia at study entry and during follow-up. Total HIV DNA, unlike the minor fraction of intact HIV DNA, correlated with prevalent cardiovascular disease, subclinical atherosclerotic disease, liver fibrosis and incident malignancies independent of circulating inflammatory markers and lowest CD4 nadir. Total HIV RNA associated with prevalent cardiovascular disease and liver fibrosis. Conclusion The HIV reservoir associated with older aging scores and long-term health outcomes in people with HIV using antiretroviral therapy, independent of inflammation and immune suppression history. Whether reservoir-reducing interventions lower the risk of non-AIDS comorbidities should be studied in people with high reservoir markers. Funding and trial registration ViiV Healthcare; 2000HIV ClinicalTrials.gov number: NTC03994835 Graphic summary Highlights HIV reservoir markers in circulating CD4 cells, including total and intact HIV DNA as well as total and unspliced HIV RNA, are highly correlated and show largely overlapping clinical and immunological characteristics. People with less favourable HIV clinical phenotypes before ART show higher levels of all measured HIV reservoir markers. Higher total HIV DNA and total HIV RNA associate with older biological aging scores and higher non-AIDS comorbidities risk after start ART. The effect of the reservoir on comorbidities is not purely dependent on systemic inflammation

research.abstract: Porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome virus (PRRSV) remains the most economically devastating pathogen of the global swine industry, with frequent genetic recombination and continuous lineage replacement driving its rapid evolution. Hubei Province, a major swine-producing hub in central China, endures substantial PRRSV disease pressure, yet the current epidemiological and evolutionary landscape of circulating strains remains poorly characterized. In this study, 1478 clinical samples were collected from 12 prefecture-level cities between 2024 and 2025 and subjected to RT-PCR detection, ORF5 sequencing, virus isolation, and complete genome analysis. The detection rate among clinical samples was 26.32%, highest in nursery pigs (32.65%). Phylogenetic analysis of 136 ORF5 sequences revealed lineage 1 dominance (66.18%), comprising NADC30-like (38.24%) and NADC34-like (27.94%) strains, followed by lineage 8 (24.26%), lineage 5 (5.15%), and lineage 3 (4.41%). Six isolates were recovered, and whole-genome analysis identified lineage-specific NSP2 deletion patterns and a recombinant strain (LW HP) bearing a JXA1-like backbone with NADC30-like insertions. Selection pressure analysis ranked Nsp2 as the least-constrained gene (dN/dS = 0.3065; purifying selection), with positively selected codons in GP5 and the NSP2 hypervariable region. These findings delineate the current epidemic status and genetic characteristics of PRRSV in central China, providing critical data for regional prevention and vaccine development.

research.abstract: Abstract T-lineage acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) is an aggressive pediatric malignancy characterized by complex heterogeneity across multiple molecular layers. Accurate subtyping is essential for understanding disease mechanisms, risk stratification, and guiding targeted therapeutic strategies. However, current diagnostic approaches are labor-intensive and time-consuming, and existing computational methods are limited by reliance on single-modality data or simple integration strategies. Effective integration of heterogeneous multi-omics data remains a major computational challenge. We present OTTER ( O ptimal T ransport-based T ranscriptomics and g E nomics R epresentation), a novel multi-modal deep learning framework that jointly models transcriptomic and genomic data for T-ALL molecular characterization. OTTER encodes each omics modality through a modality-specific encoder and aligns the resulting latent representations using Gromov-Wasserstein optimal transport (GW-OT), which preserves the internal geometric structure of each modality without requiring a shared feature space. Benchmarking tests on the Children’s Oncology Group (COG) AALL0434 cohort with >1,300 patients across 17 T-ALL subtypes suggested that OTTER significantly outperformed state-of-the-art approaches for T-ALL molecular characterization. In addition, OTTER could identify interpretable subtype-defining and omics-specific features for T-ALL. Furthermore, we have demonstrated the generalizability of OTTER by evaluating on multiple external independent clinical cohorts. In summary, OTTER provides a principled, biologically interpretable, and computationally effective framework for multi-omics driven T-ALL molecular characterization and broader cancer applications.

research.abstract: Abstract The rising threat of drug-resistant tuberculosis has renewed interest in bacteriophage therapy as an urgently needed alternative. Rational engineering of these viruses, however, requires an atomic-level understanding of virion architecture. Mycobacteriophage SWU1 belongs to subcluster A2, one of the few mycobacteriophage lineages known to infect Mycobacterium tuberculosis ( M. tuberculosis ). Using single-particle cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM), we resolved essentially the entire SWU1 virion architecture by localized reconstruction of four modules, the capsid, portal vertex, tail and baseplate, at resolutions of 3.62 Å, 3.51 Å, 3.70 Å and 3.22 Å, respectively. The T=7 capsid comprises 415 copies of an HK97-fold major capsid protein and lacks any decoration protein in density. The 12-fold portal reconciles its C5–C12 mismatch with the capsid vertex through defined, non-equivalent subunit contacts. The baseplate carries a 13-fold tail-fiber ring on a 6-fold hub, a geometry without precedent among characterized phages, established here by symmetry-free reconstruction. These findings provide the critical insights into the assembly and infection of SWU1, laying a structural foundation for the future optimization of phage-based anti-TB therapeutics.

research.abstract: Abstract Epidemiologic studies suggest that type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is associated with an increased risk of colorectal cancer (CRC). However, prior meta-analyses have relied heavily on studies published more than a decade ago and have often combined distinct epidemiologic effect measures. We conducted an updated systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies published from January 2012 through January 2026 evaluating the association between T2DM and incident CRC. PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, CENTRAL, and Scopus were searched, and eligible studies reporting associations between T2DM and CRC were included. Effect estimates were synthesized separately using random-effects models to calculate pooled estimates with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Sex-specific and leave-one-out sensitivity analyses were also conducted. Fourteen studies were included, comprising nine cohort and five case-control studies; six reported odds ratios (ORs), seven reported hazard ratios (HRs), and one reported a standardized incidence ratio (SIR). T2DM was associated with higher odds of incident CRC (OR, 1.28; 95% CI, 1.13–1.46) and a higher hazard of incident CRC (HR, 1.27; 95% CI, 1.23–1.31). The study reporting an SIR also showed higher CRC incidence among individuals with T2DM (SIR, 1.40; 95% CI, 1.39–1.45). Sex-specific analyses generally showed positive associations in both females and males, and sensitivity analyses supported the robustness of the pooled findings. Overall, T2DM was associated with an increased risk of incident CRC, with a consistent direction of association across distinct epidemiologic effect measures. These findings provide updated evidence supporting consideration of T2DM as a marker of increased CRC risk and may inform CRC prevention strategies among individuals with T2DM.

research.abstract: Summary Background Several randomised controlled trials of vitamin D supplementation for prevention of tuberculosis infection and disease have been conducted, but no individual participant data (IPD) meta-analysis has been conducted. Methods We conducted a systematic review, one-stage and two-stage IPD meta-analysis (PROSPERO CRD420251173446) of double-blind, placebo-controlled randomised trials of vitamin D supplementation for prevention of tuberculosis infection or disease. We searched MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Cochrane and ClinicalTrials.gov from inception to October 29, 2026. The co-primary outcomes were incident tuberculosis infection (evidenced by tuberculin skin test or Interferon Gamma Release Assay conversion) and incident tuberculosis disease. Mixed-effects models estimated adjusted odds ratios (aORs), accounting for trial and prespecified covariates. Prespecified subgroup analyses investigated effect modification by sex and age, body-mass index, vitamin D status, and BCG vaccination status. Findings Four trials contributed IPD for 14,619 participants. Vitamin D did not reduce risk of incident tuberculosis infection (9,557 participants; aOR 0.97, 95% CI 0.81-1.18; p=0.79) or incident tuberculosis disease (14,533 participants; aOR 0.78, 95% CI 0.56-1.10; p=0.15). There was no evidence of effect modification by participant characteristics investigated in sub-group analyses, including in participants with 25-hydroxyvitamin D <25 nmol/L (infection: aOR 0.95, 95% CI 0.67-1.34; disease: 1.01, 0.45-2.30). Serious adverse events and mortality were unaffected. Interpretation Vitamin D supplementation did not reduce the risk of incident tuberculosis infection or disease in the populations studied, either overall or within sub-groups. The 95% confidence interval of the effect estimate for prevention of tuberculosis disease remains compatible with a potentially important benefit, and further trials for this indication may be warranted.

research.abstract: DEG (Degradation of periplasmic proteins) proteases are ATP-independent serine endopeptidases found in bacteria, archaea, and eukaryotes including plants. They are considered to be key regulators of development and stress tolerance in plants. In this study, a comprehensive genome-wide analysis identified 19 serine protease-like DEG family proteins in potato (Solanum tuberosum L.), revealing their structural diversity, domain architecture, and regulatory potential. Physiochemical profiling showed a predominance of acidic isoelectric points (pI), variable protein lengths (169–1083 amino acids), and differential stability indices. Subcellular localization predicted most DEG proteases to reside in the chloroplast, with others distributed across cytoplasm, nucleus, mitochondria, and peroxisome. Domain analysis confirmed the universal presence of the trypsin domain, with varying numbers of PDZ domains and additional conserved motifs among paralogs. Evolutionary divergence analysis of StDEG genes and their orthologs from six Solanaceae species as well as Arabidopsis thaliana, Oryza sativa, and Zea mays revealed dN/dS ratios below one for all orthologous pairs, suggesting that StDEG genes have evolved under strong purifying selection and remained highly conserved throughout plant evolution. Gene ontology annotations linked DEG proteases to key biological functions including PSII repair, photoinhibition, and chloroplast organization, alongside protein catabolism and light stimulus response. Promoter analysis revealed an abundance of cis-regulatory elements (CREs), particularly light-responsive motifs, along with hormone and stress-related elements such as ABRE, ARE, and MBS. Expression profiling across eight developmental tissues demonstrated tissue-specific expression patterns, with strong transcript accumulation of selected DEG members in senescent leaf, stolon, shoot apex, and tuber. Interestingly, several splice variants showed unique expression dynamics, including stage-specific and stress-induced activation. Upon exposure to abiotic and hormonal cues, 16 DEG proteases displayed significant transcriptional modulation, particularly under light, ABA, and Zeatin treatments, with notable fold changes reaching up to 26-fold in certain variants. These findings highlight the functional versatility of DEG proteases in potato development and stress adaptation, especially their responsiveness to light and hormonal stimuli. The characterization of these proteases paves the way for future studies on their roles in crop resilience and genome editing applications.

research.abstract: Abstract Understanding variation in molecular evolutionary rates among species offers insight into the forces shaping evolution, and can inform phylogenetic models and molecular dating. Explaining this variation is challenging, however. Analyses must account for phylogenetic relationships, correlated species traits, and features of substitution rate estimates that standard approaches like phylogenetic generalised least squares (PGLS) do not address. Notably, substitution rates describe change accumulated over time along the lineages of a phylogeny, where shorter branches have higher variance in substitution rate estimation. Traits like body mass, by contrast, are instantaneous measurements and are therefore properties of nodes or tips, rather than branches. Here, we formalise an approach that overcomes these problems using phylogenetic pairwise contrasts (PPC). By comparing differences between pairs of taxa, we avoid estimating traits at internal nodes. Pairs are sampled from a phylogeny so that the edges connecting them do not overlap with any other pairs, generating comparisons that can be analysed using a linear regression. Simulations show that PPC tolerates measurement error in both traits and substitution rates while keeping its false positive rate close to nominal. PGLS, by contrast, is poorly calibrated for finding covariates of substitution rate, with up to 35% of replicates yielding p < 0.01 when no true association exists. We “ground-truth” PPC using empirical datasets, corroborating the well-established negative correlation between body size and substitution rate in flowering plants and mammals. This work offers a straightforward, reliable method for linking substitution rates to biological traits, implemented in the R package phylowise.

research.abstract: The family Noctuidae includes agricultural pests that vary in geographic distribution and host range. This study analyzed 30 mitogenomes representing 14 noctuid species; Ostrinia nubilalis (Crambidae) served as the phylogenetic outgroup. A neutrality regression based on species means revealed a modest positive association between GC3 and GC12 (R 2 = 0.3201; p = 0.03494), although it could not distinguish the respective contributions of mutation and selection. Maximum-likelihood and Bayesian analyses of 13 protein-coding genes (11,229 bp) agreed on 26 of the 28 internal groupings in the maximum-likelihood tree, including a strongly supported Spodoptera clade. Differences in deeper relationships occurred at nodes with limited support. All 13 genes had dN/dS estimates below one (0.00306-0.01691), consistent with purifying selection. Codon usage varied among gene categories, and gene-wise codon bias was not significantly associated with dN/dS. Five crop-associated species with multiple larval host plants and documented long-distance migration- Helicoverpa armigera, Athetis lepigone, Spodoptera litura, S. frugiperda, and Mamestra brassicae -fell below the fitted neutrality regression line. Whether their ecological traits relate to this pattern remains requires broader taxonomic sampling and ecological data in future investigations.

research.abstract: Zoonotic tuberculosis (zTB), caused by animal-adapted members of the Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (MTBC), is classically attributed to M. bovis but is increasingly linked to M. orygis across South Asia. Species-level MTBC identification is rarely performed in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), leaving the zTB burden poorly defined. Bangladesh has endemic bovine tuberculosis, a growing dairy sector, unpasteurised-milk consumption, and expanding captive wildlife collections, yet the evidence has not been synthesised by diagnostic reliability. This systematic evidence map aimed to collate the evidence on zTB in Bangladesh and to review the diagnostic methods used to identify animal-adapted MTBC species, particularly M. bovis and M. orygis , in livestock, wildlife, and humans. Following PRISMA 2020, we searched PubMed, Google Scholar, and BanglaJOL from the 1970s to June 2026; CAB Abstracts, Scopus, and Web of Science were not accessible. Two reviewers independently screened and appraised studies using the JBI checklist, assigning each to a five-level diagnostic evidence hierarchy (Level 1: WGS, phylogeny, RD typing, spoligotyping, or MLVA; Level 5: tuberculin skin test or serology only). These non-comparable tests precluded meta-analysis; therefore, findings are presented as an evidence map. Thirty-five studies met the inclusion criteria: 24 on prevalence in cattle/buffaloes, 10 on molecular diagnosis and characterisation in cattle, captive wildlife, and humans, and 1 specifically on molecular diagnosis and characterisation in humans. Most livestock studies used non-discriminatory tests (tuberculin skin tests, ELISA, or untyped PCR) and reported non-comparable reactor proportions of 1.2% to 33.7%. The few studies using species-level methods (Levels 1–2) confirmed M. orygis in cattle and in at least seven captive wildlife species, including monkeys, using marker-based molecular assays. Several historical reports of M. bovis were based on non-discriminatory PCR or serology, which cannot reliably distinguish among MTBC members. Human evidence was limited to three studies, including one WGS-confirmed M. orygis case identified through tuberculosis surveillance. In published reports from Bangladesh, M. orygis is the only animal-adapted MTBC member molecularly confirmed at the cattle–wildlife–human interface; existing M. bovis claims lack discriminatory support and require cautious reinterpretation. zTB surveillance should therefore move beyond an M. bovis -only framework and integrate species-level MTBC identification into a staged, resource-appropriate One Health strategy across animal, wildlife, and human health.

research.abstract: BackgroundBody mass index (BMI) does not characterize central adiposity and may obscure cardiometabolic risk among adults classified as normal weight. We evaluated associations between waist-to-height ratio (WHtR) and incident disease across the BMI spectrum and among adults with normal BMI. MethodsWe studied 308,600 adults in the All of Us Research Program. Participants with the corresponding prevalent disease were excluded separately for eight cardiometabolic outcomes. research.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Sputum culture conversion in patients with pulmonary tuberculosis (PTB) is the most important interim indicator for drug-resistant (DR) tuberculosis (TB) treatment effectiveness. Bedaquiline-based regimens offer the possibility of more effective and less toxic treatment for DR TB. Bedaquiline-based regimens have been adopted as the new standard of care for DR TB, replacing the oto-and nephrotoxic aminoglycosides. We determined the median time to sputum culture conversion (TTCC) and associated factors among RR and MDR TB patients treated with Bedaquiline-based regimens, at Mulago National Referral Hospital, Uganda. METHODS: In a longitudinal type of observational study performed at Mulago Hospital, between January 2020 and June 2023, RR and MDR TB patients' records were reviewed to obtain data on socio-demographic and clinical factors, and TTCC. The study outcome was TTCC, recorded as time from RR/MDR TB treatment initiation to sputum culture conversion, which was defined as at least 2 consecutive negative TB sputum cultures, at least 30 days apart, for a RR/MDR PTB patient who was sputum culture positive at baseline. Analysis for median TTCC was done using Kaplan-Meier analysis, and the log-logistic parametric survival regression model was used to identify predictors for TTCC. RESULTS: Of the 265 participants, 196 (74.0%) were male, with median age of 35(IQR:27-42) years. The median TTCC was 7 (IQR:4-8) weeks from treatment initiation. Grade 2 + baseline smear positivity (adjusted Time Ratio (aTR):1.24, 95% CI:1.02-1.51, p = 0.029), grade 3 + baseline smear positivity (aTR:1.62, 95% CI:1.30-2.01, p < 0.001), cavitary disease on CXR (aTR:1.36, 95% CI:1.18-1.56, p < 0.001), and pleural effusion on CXR (aTR:1.81, 95% CI:1.43-2.31, p < 0.001) significantly prolonged the TTCC. Diabetes mellitus (7/265) significantly reduced the TTCC (aTR: 0.37, 95% CI: 0.22 - 0.60, p < 0.001). CONCLUSION: The WHO long regimen (9 months) was indistinguishable from the shorter 6-months regimen for the time to culture conversion. Integration of TB screening at points of care of high-risk patients like diabetics remains important for early detection and prompt initiation of DR TB treatment for better outcomes. The TB program and clinicians should enhance and individualize support for RR/MDR TB patients with more severe disease, to ensure optimum TTCC and successful treatment outcomes. research.abstract: Purpose Patients with pulmonary tuberculosis (PTB) complicated by Klebsiella pneumoniae (KP) pneumonia are prone to acute deterioration, frequently leading to intensive care unit (ICU) admission and higher mortality. This study aimed to identify independent risk factors for ICU admission among PTB patients with KP pneumonia and develop and internally validate a concise nomogram for early risk prediction. Patients and methods This single-center retrospective cohort study enrolled 102 PTB patients complicated by KP pneumonia (50 ICU group, 52 non-ICU group) at Public Health Clinical Center of Chengdu from June 2024 to June 2025. Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (LASSO) regression with 1000-bootstrap stability assessment was used to screen candidate variables. Firth penalized logistic regression was applied to identify independent risk factors and construct the nomogram. Internal validation was performed via 1000 bootstrap resampling. Multiple statistical approaches, including the area under the curve (AUC), calibration slope, Brier score, Hosmer-Lemeshow test, calibration plots, decision curve analysis (DCA), and clinical impact curves (CIC), were adopted to quantify model discrimination, calibration, and clinical utility. Results Screened by LASSO regression and further validated with Firth logistic regression, six-month pre-admission Gram-negative bacterial infection history, pre-admission carbapenem exposure within six months, respiratory virus infection, fungal infection, and systemic glucocorticoid use at admission constituted independent risk factors for ICU admission (all P). The nomogram had an apparent AUC of 0.935 and bootstrap-corrected AUC of 0.920 (optimism = 0.015), suggesting minimal overfitting within the development cohort, though external validation is needed to confirm generalizability. The apparent and optimism-corrected calibration slopes were 1.138 and 0.914, respectively. The apparent Brier score was 0.103, and the corrected Brier score was 0.083. The Hosmer-Lemeshow test indicated favorable calibration (P=0.832). DCA and CIC confirmed stable clinical net benefit across reasonable threshold probabilities. Conclusion Constructed from five readily-available clinical variables, this nomogram shows good discrimination and satisfactory calibration for predicting ICU-admission risk in PTB patients with KP pneumonia. External validation is still needed to verify its generalizability. Before such validation is performed, the tool should serve only as a supportive risk-stratification aid instead of a standalone clinical decision-making instrument. It may help identify patients who deserve intensified monitoring owing to high risk of clinical deterioration.

research.abstract: Abstract The Wnt gene family plays a central role in vertebrate development, yet its evolutionary dynamics across lineages remain largely unexplored. Here, we present the most comprehensive analysis of Wnt gene evolution in vertebrates to date, leveraging a large-scale comparative genomics approach of 38,886 Wnt gene sequences mined from 1,961 species. We first investigate overall patterns of gene retention, duplication, and loss, and then focus specifically on the impact of whole-genome duplications (WGDs). We uncover striking variation in Wnt gene repertoire sizes, with ray-finned fishes (Actinopterygii) exhibiting the largest repertoires – even after excluding taxa with recent WGDs. Notably, we identify extreme expansions in polyploid cyprinids, including an octoploid hybrid harbouring 99 Wnt genes, the highest number observed. Unexpectedly elevated Wnt copy numbers in diploid species, such as in the Antarctic lanternfish (Electrona antarctica) and the brook lamprey (Lethenteron reissneri), point to lineage-specific expansions, although the potential adaptive significance of these expansions remains to be tested. Evolutionary rate analyses reveal that certain Wnt clades – especially Wnt8 and Wnt16 – exhibit elevated dN/dS ratios and high birth–death rates, consistent with repeated episodes of relaxed constraint and/or adaptive diversification. Contrary to our expectations, there was no relationship between developmental expression timing and evolutionary rates, suggesting pleiotropic regulation and functional redundancy of Wnt genes. Altogether, our findings reveal widespread variation in Wnt copy number and turnover among lineages, shaped by both genome duplication history and divergent evolutionary trajectories. This work provides a high-resolution framework for understanding the molecular evolution of a key developmental toolkit and highlights candidate genes for future studies of vertebrate eco-morphological diversity.

research.abstract: Abstract Complex genomic rearrangements (CGRs) are hallmarks of tumor genomes, yet their architectures and origins remain poorly understood. We utilized optical mapping to profile the genomic landscapes of lung tissues across various stages - from normal and benign lesions to advanced carcinomas - to characterize genome disorganization during carcinogenesis. We developed omcplR to resolve the CGR architectures and predict their genesis using the genome-graph framework. Our findings reveal that many CGRs arise from hierarchical combinations of localized structural variations that are unlikely due to break-fusion-bridge, chromothripsis, or chromoplexy. We termed this process chromodiadochi: a cascade of nested rearrangements accumulating over multiple generations during carcinogenesis. Early intra-chromosomal junctions in CGRs typically localized within specific chromatin domains, while late junctions in advanced tumors occurred in more heterogeneous contexts and showed signs of positive selection. A composite signature of genomic alterations, including the CGRs, captures the trajectory of progressive genomic structural disorganization and instability from benign tissue to malignancy.

research.abstract: INTRODUCTION: TB (tuberculosis) due to Mycobacterium tuberculosis continues to be a significant worldwide health issue. Timely and reliable diagnostic tests will improve treatment outcomes and reduce the spread of disease. Traditional TB diagnostics currently available, such as smear microscopy and culture, have significant limitations with regard to sensitivity and turnaround times, especially for smear-negative cases and for tuberculosis in extrapulmonary locations. OBJECTIVES: The purpose of this review is to analyze the evolution of TB diagnostics from traditional microbiology to new molecular diagnostic methods (including CRISPR, biosensor technology, and microfluidic methods), including an assessment of their diagnostic testing performance, feasibility, and potential for the future. METHODS: The systematic narrative review aimed to systematically assess literature published from 2020 to 2025 retrieved from PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, ScienceDirect, and Google Scholar. The review was carried out according to the PRISMA guidelines and included 89 studies after screening and assessing for eligibility. The data were analysed qualitatively (i.e., through thematic analysis) by comparing data from conventional, molecular, and next-generation diagnostic methods. RESULTS: Molecular tests (e.g., GeneXpert, Line Probe Assays, PCR, and Whole Genome Sequencing) provide greater sensitivity and specificity than traditional methods and allow for faster diagnosis. Additionally, newer CRISPR-based tests, biosensors, and microfluidic devices hold promise for rapid, portable, point-of-care diagnosis of tuberculosis. DISCUSSION: The findings indicate that molecular diagnostics improve rapid detection and drug-resistance profiling, while CRISPR and biosensor platforms offer potential for rapid point-of-care testing. However, affordability, infrastructure, clinical validation, and scalability remain important barriers. CONCLUSION: The use of molecular diagnostic testing, CRISPR technology, biosensors, artificial intelligence, and portable platforms will dramatically enhance existing TB surveillance systems and strategies for controlling the disease globally.

research.abstract: Tuberculosis (TB), caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis , remains a major global health challenge, further exacerbated by the rapid emergence of drug-resistant strains. Despite continuous efforts, the discovery of novel anti-TB agents has lagged behind the evolution of resistance, largely due to the limitations of conventional experimental pipelines and the growing biological complexity of the pathogen. In recent years, computational drug discovery approaches—including virtual screening, artificial intelligence (AI)-driven modeling, and hybrid computational frameworks—have substantially expanded the chemical space accessible for early-stage anti-TB research. However, their translational success remains limited. This discrepancy reflects a fundamental mismatch between target-centric computational paradigms and the multi-scale biological constraints of Mtb , including permeability barriers, efflux mechanisms, metabolic state heterogeneity, lesion-level pharmacokinetics, and regimen-dependent therapeutic effects. This review critically evaluates current computational strategies for anti-TB drug screening, with particular emphasis on their performance under TB-specific biological and resistance constraints. We further explore computational approaches designed to address drug-resistant Mtb , including resistance-aware compound design, host-directed therapy, and combination regimen modeling. Finally, we explore key limitations in current computational pipelines, including challenges in data quality, biological integration, and regimen-level modeling, and propose a shift toward biologically grounded, regimen-aware, and systems-level frameworks. Bridging the gap between in silico prediction and clinical efficacy will require integrating multi-scale biological realism into computational pipelines, enabling more reliable translation of computational advances into effective anti-TB therapeutics.

research.abstract: Computing phylogenetic likelihoods becomes challenging when the continuous-time Markov chain has a large state space. At each branch, pruning algorithms require terms of the form $e^{Q t}\cdot B$, where $Q$ is an $S \times S$ rate matrix (e.g., for $S$ states), $t$ is a branch length, and the columns of matrix $B$ (e.g., $B \in \mathbb{R}_{+}^{S \times L}$) are partial-likelihood vectors for $L$ site patterns. Many implementations calculate the dense transition matrix $P(t)=e^{Q t}$ via eigendecomposition and multiply it by $B$. This strategy is efficient for small state spaces, but it can be inefficient for large sparse rate matrices because forming $P(t)$ or its eigen vector matrices destroys sparsity and its cost may not be well amortized when $L$ is small. We implement an alternative likelihood kernel based on the Al-Mohy and Higham (2011) algorithm for computing the action of the matrix exponential directly, avoiding explicit construction of $P(t)$ or its eigen vector matrices. The resulting method takes full advantage of the sparsity of $Q$. We implement this method as a CPU-based extension to the BEAGLE library and evaluate it on two large-state molecular models: a Markov-modulated codon model of heterotachy with $M$ selective regimes and $61\cdot M$ possible states, and a codon-pair model of interlocus gene conversion between two paralogs with $61^2=3\,721$ possible states. Our results characterize when action-based likelihood computation improves performance over calculating $e^{Q t}$ directly. We show that this method enables fast, scalable inference for complex models, removing a key computational barrier to the study of evolution with large state space models.

research.abstract: Abstract A vast degree of phenotypic variation can be seen across lineages of eukaryotes. Although at least part of this diversity has a genomic basis, it is unclear whether there are broad-scale links that can be detected between rates of genomic and phenotypic evolution. The presence of a correlation would imply the action of shared drivers, such as mutational or adaptive processes that occur on a genome- and organism-wide scale. We investigated this question by using a phylogenetic approach to test for correlations between molecular and morphological evolutionary rates. We analysed 60 data sets of combined nucleotide sequences and discrete morphological characters, representing a diverse range of eukaryotes. Using a maximum-likelihood phylogenetic approach based on sister-pair contrasts, we found very little evidence of any link between rates of molecular and morphological evolution, a striking result given the scale and taxonomic breadth of our analyses. Our results point to contrasting evolutionary dynamics underlying genomes and phenotypic traits; these have led to greater variation in morphological evolutionary rates across lineages, whereas molecular evolution is more clocklike. Our study reveals the discrepancies in evolutionary drivers that act at the genomic and phenotypic levels across the eukaryotic Tree of Life.

research.abstract: Phylogenetic trees are hybrid objects: branch lengths vary continuously, while topologies change discretely through edge contractions and expansions. Billera-Holmes-Vogtmann (BHV) tree space provides a canonical geometry for this structure, representing each resolved topology as a Euclidean orthant and topological changes as motion across shared lower-dimensional boundaries. We introduce PhylaFlow, a hybrid flow-matching model that learns posterior-basin transport in BHV tree space. PhylaFlow is trained on BHV geodesic paths from random starting trees to short-run posterior samples, coupling continuous branch-length motion within orthants with learned boundary events and discrete topology transitions. We evaluate the learned geometry operationally: if the flow reaches posterior-relevant regions, finite-budget Bayesian refinement initialized from, or guided by, its terminal trees should recover posterior-supported topologies more efficiently. Across DS1-DS8 phylogenetic posterior benchmarks, PhylaFlow substantially reduces initial Tree-KL relative to classical initializers. After finite-budget MrBayes refinement, direct PhylaFlow improves early and intermediate topology-recovery trajectories on most datasets, while split-guided PhylaFlow-MCMC obtains the strongest hard-case results. The best PhylaFlow variant outperforms short-warmup on seven of eight datasets and PhyloGFN on five of eight under the same refinement budget. In a joint sequence-conditioned experiment, sequence embeddings steer posterior split recovery, although exact posterior topology recovery remains preliminary. These results show that hybrid flow matching can learn actionable transport in BHV tree space and provide a geometry-aware proposal mechanism for Bayesian phylogenetic inference.

research.abstract: Characium and Characium -like algae represent a taxonomically challenging group within Chlorophyceae. Due to their high phenotypic plasticity and convergent morphology, their true evolutionary relationships have long remained unresolved, and the lack of genomic resources has further hindered taxonomic revision. We sequenced and assembled seven complete chloroplast genomes from Characium and morphologically similar taxa and documented their detailed cell morphology. Comparative genomic analyses revealed that while most genomes retained the typical quadripartite structure, they exhibited significant structural variation, including gene rearrangements and diverse IR expansions/contractions. Furthermore, phylogenetic analyses based on 64 protein-coding genes successfully resolved the long-standing taxonomic ambiguity of Characium and Characium -like algae, placing the strains into three distinct, well-supported clades within Sphaeropleales and Volvocales. Branch-site tests identified a small set of positively selected genes, mainly related to photosynthesis, proteolysis, and plastid gene expression, suggesting that adaptive processes may have contributed to chloroplast genome diversity in these algae. This study establishes the first clear phylogenomic framework for these lineages, revealing distinct evolutionary patterns of gene loss and structural rearrangement that align with the newly resolved clades. It also provides an important basis for advancing studies on chloroplast genome evolution within Chlorophyceae.

research.abstract: Abstract A longstanding goal in human genetics is to prioritize noncoding loci that, when disrupted, lead to developmental disorders and other Mendelian traits. In pursuit of this goal, multiple metrics have been developed to distinguish neutrally evolving sequences from those subjected to purifying selection. These metrics are commonly evaluated genome-wide, e.g., by computing a precision-recall curve on windows tiling the entire noncoding genome. Here, we identify parts of the noncoding genome where these metrics are distorted due to “bias” in the underlying models of neutral genetic variation and underperform due to a low “signal-to-noise ratio” in the genetic data. The most extreme effects are found for Gnocchi (Chen et al. 2024), the performance of which declines as GC content increases. We trace the source of the bias in Gnocchi to a mismatch between the training set of de novo mutations (DNMs) used to adjust expected SNP counts and the genomic windows on which those expected counts are computed. Resolving that mismatch produces a more calibrated version of Gnocchi, significantly improving its interpretability in applications. Looking forward, we suggest annotating constraint scores of noncoding genomic intervals with robust measures of the bias of the corresponding model, allowing users to gauge confidence in those scores.

research.abstract: Uropathogenic Escherichia coli (UPEC) presents a significant therapeutic challenge due to increasing multidrug resistance (MDR). While acquired resistance mechanisms are well-documented, the genetic variability of intrinsic efflux pumps like EmrD remains less characterized. This study investigated the genomic diversity and structural conservation of the EmrD transporter in ten clinical MDR isolates from the Kurdistan Region, Iraq. Isolates were screened for the emrD and β-lactamase genes, followed by emrD sequencing, phylogenetic analysis, and in silico protein modeling. Results confirmed the universal presence of emrD alongside multiple resistance genes. Phylogenetic analysis identified notable local genetic diversity, including a highly divergent lineage (DUH 11). Protein modeling mapped non-synonymous substitutions to transmembrane helices 6 and 12, regions critical for the "rocker-switch" conformational changes required for substrate translocation. These findings suggest that while EmrD is a stable component of the MDR machinery, localized genomic divergence may potentially influence efflux efficiency among clinical lineages, warranting future functional validation.

research.abstract: Tuberculosis (TB) remains the leading infectious killer worldwide. Brazil is among the 30 high-burden TB countries, however, genomic surveillance of Mycobacterium tuberculosis strains remains limited. We analyzed a convenience sample of 350 clinical isolates collected between 2016 and 2021 in metropolitan Rio de Janeiro to investigate genomic diversity, drug resistance and transmission dynamics. Among the isolates, 302 were phenotypically susceptible, while 48 showed resistance to at least one drug, including 35 multidrug-resistant (MDR) cases. Whole-genome sequencing predictions showed high concordance with phenotypic drug susceptibility testing (rifampicin 99%, isoniazid 99%, ethambutol 98%, streptomycin 97%). The most common resistance mutations were katG Ser315Thr and rpoB Ser450Leu. All isolates belonged to Lineage 4, predominantly sub-lineages 4.1 (Haarlem) and 4.3 (Latin American-Mediterranean). Despite incomplete sampling, genomic analysis identified 28 transmission clusters involving 23.2% of isolates, including a large MDR-TB cluster in the Tijuca neighborhood. Multi-year clusters indicated continued detection of closely related isolates over time, suggesting the persistence of related genomic lineages. No association was observed between resistance-associated mutations and treatment outcomes, although these analyses were likely underpowered to detect such associations. These findings highlight the need to strengthen genomic surveillance, molecular diagnostics, contact tracing, and treatment follow-up to control TB in the region.

research.abstract: Tuberculosis (TB) diagnosis remains challenging, particularly for extrapulmonary TB (EPTB), where invasive sampling, low bacillary burden, and limited sensitivity of nucleic acid-based tests in peripheral specimens hinder timely detection. Here, we report an immunology-driven strategy for biomarker discovery and development of a peptide-based serological assay targeting Mycobacterium tuberculosis zinc metalloprotease-1 (Zmp1). Based on the principle that antigenic regions containing overlapping B-cell and CD4⁺T-cell epitopes can promote strong antibody responses through linked recognition and cognate T-cell help, we used an immunoinformatics pipeline to identify two nested immunodominant Zmp1 peptide regions, Mtb-Zp-NT and Mtb-Zp-CT, enriched for overlapping B- and T-cell epitopes.Their diagnostic potential was evaluated using ELISA-based serological assays. A blinded pilot study (N = 137) demonstrated clear discrimination between active TB and TB-recovered individuals. An expanded validation cohort (N = 875), identified from screening approximately 6,086 individuals, included pulmonary TB (PTB), EPTB, TB-recovered individuals, household contacts, non-specific infection/inflammation, and healthy controls. Receiver operating characteristic analyses, supported by DeLong and bootstrap comparisons, demonstrated superior diagnostic performance of the peptide assays compared with Mtb-FL-Zmp1. Mtb-Zp-CT showed the highest accuracy (AUC = 0.93), with > 93% specificity and ~ 76% sensitivity.These findings establish immunologically optimized Zmp1 peptides as promising serological biomarkers for TB, including EPTB. Although further optimization may be required to meet WHO target product profiles, their high specificity supports potential use as an adjunctive diagnostic, particularly for EPTB, and as components of future multi-antigen panels. More broadly, this study demonstrates how mechanistically informed epitope selection can facilitate translation of pathogen-specific immune signatures into minimally invasive diagnostic platforms.

research.abstract: Abstract Background The Streptococcus anginosus group (SAG) ( S. anginosus, S. intermedius, and S. constellatus ) causes serious, potentially life-threatening, invasive infections, often in otherwise healthy individuals. However, the group’s diversity is still poorly understood, and with it, the ability to identify prognostic markers of severe disease. Methods Long-read sequencing produced closed genomes for 29 isolates from 25 patients hospitalised primarily for invasive SAG infections, and 21 isolates from 20 non-hospitalised controls. Genomes were classified with GTDB-Tk and combined with 211 reference genomes. After dereplication, 207 SAG genomes (38 isolate, 169 reference) representing 206 strains were analysed using: GTDB classification, average nucleotide identity, multi-marker and core-genome SNP phylogenies, recombination-aware analyses, mobilome, CAZyme and gapseq metabolic profiling, and lineage-aware genome-wide association testing for invasive phenotype. Results Agreement between GTDB-Tk and MALDI-TOF taxonomic classifications was low (42.8%), including two S. massiliensis cases mis-identified by MALDI-TOF as SAG. S. anginosus resolved into four taxa ( S. anginosus , S. hominis , S. whileyi and S. vaginalis ). Phylogenies based on core genome single-nucleotide polymorphisms resolved these species into distinct clades, whereas 16S rRNA gene and multilocus sequence analysis phylogenies did not. The four ex- S. anginosus taxa showed a gradient of genomic cohesion, with S. vaginalis being near-clonal, in contrast to S. anginosus, which shared high levels of sequence ancestry with other neighbouring taxa. Carbohydrate utilisation was strongly lineage-associated, as was propensity for invasive disease. A ∼15Kbp glycosaminoglycan utilisation locus was found in the three taxa of highest disease severity propensity ( S. intermedius, S. constellatus, S. whileyi ) which predicts a direct host glycosaminoglycan feeding mechanism that may contribute to invasive disease. No single functional feature, gene or core-genome SNP was associated with invasiveness however after lineage-adjustment. Combined feature analysis suggests S. vaginalis has undergone a niche restriction and has evolved for a primary existence in the female urogenital tract. Conclusions Under-reported species may be mis-diagnosed as SAG invasive infections. SAG is more diverse than its current three-species definition, with the conventional S. anginosus species proposed to be classed into a complex of four distinct taxa. Invasive capacity appears to be an emergent system-level property rather than from individual features.

research.abstract: Large-scale pharmacogenomic screens provide rich drug-sensitivity measurements in cancer cell lines, but transferring these measurements to patient tumours remains limited by biological heterogeneity and cross-domain distribution shift. Existing machine learning approaches, including adversarial autoencoder and domain adaptation, address this gap by learning shared latent representations between preclinical models and patient samples. However, alignment without explicit biological constraints can produce unreliable representations when cancer lineage structure and clinically relevant patient heterogeneity are not preserved. Here, we introduce MODAE+, a pan-cancer multi-objective deep learning domain adaptation framework that jointly balances domain alignment, deconfounding, drug-response prediction, survival prediction, and cancer-lineage classification across 9,696 TCGA tumours, 1,293 CCLE cancer cell lines, and CTRP sensitivity profiles for 544 compounds in 738 matched cell lines. This multi-objective design improved cross-domain alignment while preserving cancer-lineage organization and patient heterogeneity. For drugs shared between the pharmacogenomic screen and TCGA treatment records, MODAE+ predicted sensitivity was significantly associated with overall survival among patients who received each drug in 46.3% of evaluated cancer-drug pairs by log-rank testing and 41.5% by multivariable Cox analysis. Biological validation across four curated drug-gene resources identified significant expression differences exceeding 1.5-fold for 34.9-64.4% of drugs in pan-cancer analyses, based on the lowest-p-value annotated gene per drug. Drug-class-specific patterns involved intended molecular targets for targeted therapies and predominantly transport, metabolism, detoxification and resistance-related genes for classical chemotherapies. As an additional validation, we derived pretreatment responder-nonresponder gene-expression signatures from 13 external breast cancer datasets and evaluated their concordance with MODAE+ predictions across 69 signature-drug comparisons in TCGA patients treated with paclitaxel or doxorubicin. Consensus signature scores showed Spearman correlations of 0.791 with predicted paclitaxel sensitivity and 0.724 with predicted doxorubicin sensitivity, averaging 0.758 across the two drugs. Together, these complementary analyses provide supporting evidence for the clinical relevance and biological consistency of MODAE+ predictions, suggesting their potential to identify drug-sensitive tumour subgroups and generate hypotheses about mechanisms of drug resistance.

research.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To determine the proportion of resistance to five new and repurposed drugs (NRDs), identify risk factors for resistance, and characterize associated genetic mutations and transmission among people with multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant TB (MDR/RR-TB) in Shenzhen, China. METHODS: Clinical isolates were collected from all people with MDR/RR-TB admitted to Shenzhen Third People's Hospital between January 2022 and December 2024. The minimum inhibitory concentrations of five NRDs - bedaquiline (BDQ), clofazimine (CFZ), delamanid (DLM), pretomanid (PMD) and linezolid (LZD) - were determined using the broth microdilution method. Risk factors for NRD resistance were identified using Firth's penalized logistic regression. Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) was performed on 99 isolates, including all NRD-resistant strains and randomly selected susceptible strains, to analyze resistance-conferring mutations, phylogeny, and clustering. RESULTS: Among 561 people with MDR/RR-TB, resistance proportions were BDQ 4.3%, CFZ 3.6%, DLM 1.1%, PMD 1.1% and LZD 1.4%. Prior NRD exposure (aOR=4.96; 95% CI, 1.95-12.61; P=0.001) and male gender (aOR=3.64; 95% CI, 1.15-11.56; P=0.028) showed strong positive associations with NRD resistance. BDQ exposure posed a higher risk of both BDQ- and CFZ-resistance than CFZ exposure. Based on the WHO mutation catalogue, WGS predicted NRD resistance with 100% specificity, sensitivity ranged from 16.7% to 75.0%. Notably, 37.5%-66.7% of resistant cases had no prior NRD exposure, and clustered isolates indicated transmitted resistance. CONCLUSION: NRD resistance among MDR/RR-TB patients in Shenzhen remains low. Although prior drug exposure is the primary risk factor, there is also evidence of transmitted resistance. NRD surveillance is essential to guide treatment and control transmission.

research.abstract: Background: Cancer of unknown primary (CUP) is a metastatic, heterogeneous malignancy accounting for 2-5% of cancer diagnoses globally. Failure to identify the primary site precludes tumor-type-specific therapy and, together with an aggressive clinical course, contributes to poor survival. The biological mechanisms driving these behaviors remain poorly understood. A deeper understanding of CUP biology is therefore essential to improve diagnostic precision and therapeutic strategies. To address this knowledge gap, we comprehensively characterized the multi-omics landscape of CUP and identified biological and potentially therapeutic targets beyond tissue-of-origin (ToO) assignment. Methods: Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) data from 283 CUP patients were analyzed for ToO predictions, mutational signatures, driver alterations, genetic immune escape (GIE), and clinically actionable alterations. Matched RNA-sequencing (RNA-seq) data from 79 cases were used to characterize functional gene expression signatures and define transcriptomic subtypes. Clinical, WGS, and RNA-seq data were integrated via weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA). Results: High-confidence ToO predictions (likelihood >80%) were obtained for 58% of CUPs, most commonly predicting lung, gastrointestinal, and biliary tract origins. Mutational signatures clustering revealed four subgroups dominated by tobacco smoking, defective DNA mismatch repair (dMMR), UV exposure, and APOBEC activity, while a fifth group, comprising most tumors (n=169; 60%), showed mixed mutational processes. The cohort also frequently exhibited mutations in established cancer driver genes, including TP53, CDKN2A, KRAS, and epigenetic modifiers ARID1A, SMARCA4, and ARID2. GIE alterations occurred in 35% of tumors, mostly involving HLA-I genes. Transcriptomic profiling defined five subtypes with different degrees of immune infiltration, fibrosis, and tumor proliferation. These subtypes were not significantly associated with clinical or genomic features, indicating that the tumor microenvironment (TME) represents another layer of CUP heterogeneity. WGCNA further linked proliferative programs to cell-cycle, DNA-replication, and neuroendocrine features. WGS data identified potentially targetable alterations in 64% of the CUP patients. Conclusions: CUP comprises biologically heterogeneous tumors with diverse predicted origins, mutational histories, and TME subtypes. Transcriptomic profiling and integrated genomics suggest that immune escape and rapid proliferation contribute to the clinical aggressive behavior. Together, these findings provide a molecular framework for understanding CUP heterogeneity and support therapeutic stratification by both ToO predictions and tumor-specific molecular alterations.
