research.abstract: Abstract Comparative genomic data can be used to look for substitutions in coding sequences that are associated with the variation of a particular phenotypic trait. A few statistical methods have been proposed to do so for phenotypes represented by discrete values. For continuous traits, no such statistical approach has been proposed, and researchers have resorted to sensible but uncharacterized criteria. Here, we investigate a phylogenetic model for coding sequences where amino acid preferences at a site are given by a continuous function of a quantitative trait. This function is inferred from the amino acids and the trait values in extant species and requires inferred point estimates of ancestral values of the trait at internal nodes. For detecting sites whose evolution is associated with this trait, we use a significance test against the hypothesis that amino acid preference does not depend on the trait. This procedure is compared to simpler strategies on simulated alignments. It displays an increased recall for low false positive rates, which is of special importance for performing whole-genome scans. This comes however at a much higher computational cost, and we suggest using a simple test to filter promising candidate sites. We then revisit a dataset of alignments for 62 species of mammals, using longevity as a phenotypic trait. We apply our method to three protein families that have previously been proposed to display sites associated with variation in lifespan in mammals. Using a graphical representation extracted from the detailed phylogenetic analysis of candidate sites, we suggest that the evidence for this in the sequence data alone is weak. The proposed method has been added to our Pelican software. It is available at https://gitlab.in2p3.fr/phoogle/pelican and can now be used with both discrete and continuous phenotypes to search for sites associated with phenotypic variation, on data sets with thousands of alignments.

research.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Thyroid dysfunction is a common endocrine comorbidity in type 1 diabetes (T1D), yet most evidence on its burden and biochemical patterns comes from higher-income settings. Data among African children and young adults with T1D remain limited. Objective To determine the prevalence and pattern of thyroid dysfunction and examine demographic and diabetes-related factors associated with thyroid dysfunction among children and young adults with T1D in Kenya. Methods We conducted a multicentre cross-sectional study among children and young adults with T1D aged ≤34 years attending four diabetes clinics in Kenya. Serum thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) and free thyroxine (FT4) were measured. Thyroid status was classified as euthyroidism (normal TSH and FT4), subclinical hypothyroidism (elevated TSH with normal FT4), overt hypothyroidism (elevated TSH with low FT4), subclinical hyperthyroidism (low TSH with normal FT4), overt hyperthyroidism (low TSH with elevated FT4), or discordant TSH–FT4 profiles that did not meet these predefined biochemical categories. Prevalence estimates with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated, and multivariable logistic regression examined associations with age, sex and duration of diabetes. Results Among 244 participants with paired TSH and FT4 measurements, 77.5% (n=189) were euthyroid. Twenty-seven participants (11.1%; 95% CI 7.7–15.6%) had biochemically defined thyroid dysfunction: 18 (7.4%) had subclinical hypothyroidism, 5 (2.0%) overt hypothyroidism, and 4 (1.6%) subclinical hyperthyroidism. No overt hyperthyroidism was identified. An additional 28 participants (11.5%) had discordant TSH–FT4 profiles. Hypothyroidism accounted for 85.2% of biochemically defined thyroid dysfunction and was predominantly subclinical (78.3%). Age, sex and duration of diabetes were not significantly associated with thyroid dysfunction in adjusted analyses. Conclusion Thyroid dysfunction affected approximately one in nine Kenyan children and young adults with T1D and was predominantly hypothyroid, particularly subclinical hypothyroidism. Discordant TSH–FT4 profiles were also frequent, underscoring the importance of careful biochemical classification and confirmation of abnormal thyroid-function tests.

We generated paired blood- and nasal-derived genomes from the MV Hondius outbreak and integrated them with a segment-linked collection of human- and rodent-derived ANDV sequences, including incomplete genomes. We developed a linkage-informed missing-segment framework that preserves isolate identity, sampling time, and cross-segment placement without imputing nucleotide states, enabling sensitivity analyses of patchy segment coverage. Across five human outbreaks, dated phylogenies placed outbreak lineages independently within geographically structured reservoir diversity, with closest sampled ancestry predating detection. Time-dependent-rate analyses indicated a deeper reservoir-associated history, while mutation reconstruction, selection tests, branch-rate comparisons, and structural mapping found no recurrent adaptive transition preceding human transmission. MV Hondius samples showed minimal consensus-level diversification. These results shift attention from repeated recent adaptation toward deeper lineage properties and ecological opportunity.

research.abstract: Abstract Objective To assess stakeholder acceptability of and preferences for long-acting injectables (LAIs) for tuberculosis (TB) treatment and prevention across World Health Organization regions to inform product development and implementation. Methods We conducted a sequential explanatory mixed-methods study of survey data and qualitative focus group discussions (FGDs). Online surveys assessed perceptions and acceptance of LAIs among two groups: TB programme managers, civil society members and healthcare workers (Survey A), and community members and persons affected by TB (Survey B). Using purposive sampling, survey participants were invited to join FGDs to explore survey findings. Survey data were analysed using descriptive statistics, ordinal logistic regression with stepwise AIC selection, and one-sample proportion tests. FGD transcripts were analysed using modified framework analysis. Findings Among 310 participants (102 Survey A; 208 Survey B), 83% (n=256) favoured LAIs over standard oral TB treatment. Compared with six months of daily oral treatment, 69% preferred a three-month regimen comprising one month of daily oral treatment followed by four injections per monthly visit for two months, while 80% preferred the corresponding regimen with two injections per visit. For prevention, 79% preferred a single injection over one month of oral treatment. In Survey B, interest varied according to lived TB experience, with FGDs suggesting that previous negative experiences with injectables may have contributed to this variation. Conclusion Interest in LAIs for TB treatment and prevention was high, but lower among participants with lived TB experience. Product development and implementation should address concerns about injectables and side effects while preserving patient choice and agency.

research.abstract: Background Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), the causative agent of tuberculosis (TB) is able to survive and replicate within host cells of the myeloid cell lineage, a critical step in the development of active TB, achieved through multiple immune evasion mechanisms. TRPML1 (Mucolipin 1), a non-selective Ca 2+ ion channel belonging to the TRP superfamily, is predominantly expressed in innate immune cells and is localized intracellularly along the endosomal–lysosomal continuum. TRPML1-mediated Ca 2+ signalling is vital for lysosomal biogenesis and trafficking processes essential for effective immune responses. The mechanisms regulating TRPML1 channel function in myeloid cells during mycobacterial infection remain poorly characterized. Methods During in vitro infection, TRPML1 expression was modulated in a time-dependent manner by Mtb and M. bovis BCG in murine macrophages, as well as in human neutrophils (PMNs) and macrophages (MDMs). Using pharmacological modulation of TRPML1 channel activity, we observed alterations in intracellular Ca 2+ concentrations following Mtb infection. Results Here, we describe distinct TRPML1 expression patterns in granulomas from TB patients who had completed treatment for active TB, suggesting a potential role for TRPML1 in pathogenesis. We further demonstrate that Mtb infection is associated with altered TRPML1 expression and intracellular Ca 2+ homeostasis, accompanied by changes in ROS production, necrotic cell death and enhanced mycobacterial survival within host cells. Treatment of PMN-MDM cocultures with a TRPML1 antagonist, but not an agonist, was associated with increased reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels and necrotic cell death. Discussion Here, we show that Mtb-mediated disruption of TRPML1 function is associated with altered intracellular Ca 2+ homeostasis and may contribute to impaired phagosome maturation, a process previously linked to TRPML1-dependent endolysosomal function, thereby potentially favoring mycobacterial survival within host cells. These findings suggest that Mtb-induced alterations in TRPML1 associated cellular Ca²⁺ homeostasis may impair Ca²⁺-dependent ROS production and cell death, potentially affecting intracellular Mtb survival. Our findings support a role for TRPML1 in maintaining myeloid cell Ca²⁺ homeostasis and suggest that TRPML1 may contribute to the innate immune response to Mtb infection.

research.abstract: Abstract In April-July 2026, Andes virus (ANDV) caused an outbreak aboard the MV Hondius cruise ship resulting in 12 confirmed cases and three deaths. Before symptom onset, the index case had travelled through hantavirus-endemic regions of Chile and Argentina, leaving the geographic origin of infection unresolved. We conducted phylogenetic and phylogeographic analyses using newly generated ANDV genomes from human cases and rodent reservoirs to investigate the likely origin of the outbreak. Through phylogenetic analyses, we show that the outbreak genome falls within a geographically structured lineage spanning southern Chile and Argentine Andean Patagonia. Using phylogeographic reconstructions across all three segments, integrated with the index case’s travel itinerary, we identified the Toltén-Lanco area of southern Chile as the most likely geographic origin of the outbreak genome, with two candidate locations accounting for >98% of the posterior support. However, the index case visited this area 62-66 days before symptom onset, exceeding the conventionally reported ANDV incubation period of 7-42 days. Thus, while genomic evidence supports a southern Chilean origin of the outbreak genome, the timing and circumstances of transmission to the index case remain unresolved.

research.abstract: Abstract Ancestral sequences and substitution histories are usually averaged out in phylogenetic inference and are therefore not reported to the user. However, they can be recovered through ancestral sequence reconstruction (ASR) and stochastic character mapping. By implementing and validating a new ASR and stochastic mapping package compatible with both single-locus and multispecies coalescent analysis, we show how reconstructing substitution histories can enhance the information gained about the tempo and mode of molecular evolution. We observe that known substitution histories (simulated and empirical) are recovered more accurately and precisely on time trees compared with unconstrained and non-ultrametric substitution trees that lack temporal directionality (maximum likelihood and Bayesian). We show that codon-partition models with site-rate heterogeneity, based on the four nucleotide characters, can effectively approximate the histories of synonymous and non-synonymous change, while requiring far less runtime than computationally demanding codon models that require 61 characters. In turn, this provides low-bias estimation of dN/dS that is robust to non-stationarity in GC content, codon usage bias, and nucleotide exchangeability rates. Lastly, using three case studies, we demonstrate how the approach can recover expected patterns in molecular evolution and pathogen transmission: that i) smaller-bodied mammalian species tend to have faster synonymous substitution rates than larger relatives, ii) amino acid substitutions are correlated with 3Di structural changes in aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases, and iii) influenza A virus spread more frequently to nearby locations than distant ones, in a major H3N2 outbreak in New Zealand. These three trends were more pronounced when based on count estimates derived from stochastic mapping, relative to parametric rates and distances. Our open-source code comes with a user-friendly graphical interface, as the BeastMap package for BEAST 2; supporting a wide range of clock, site, and tree models and data types – including insertions and deletions – within a Bayesian phylogenetic framework.

research.abstract: Abstract Background Although the majority of structural variant (SV) workflows have been derived based on whole genome sequencing (WGS) data, they continue to be applied to whole exome sequence (WES) data for which many studies have evaluated their performance in cancer. An equally important consideration that has not been well studied is the impact of cancer context specific features among WGS-derived SV callers applied to WES data. Like personalized medicine, not all SV callers are alike and optimal for use with all cancer types and sequence data types. In addition to sequencing related data features, cancer types have embedded features withing the sequencing data that should be considered. Herein, we performed an analysis of SV heterogeneity among WGS-derived SV callers to WES data in multiple myeloma (MM), a cancer known for its genetically heterogeneous nature. Using WES data derived from a panel of 67 Multiple Myeloma (MM) cell lines, we evaluated seven WGS-derived SV detection tools (Delly, SvABA, BreakDancer, Smoove, LUMPY and Manta) for their ability to identify cytogenetically known genetic abnormalities and to characterize overall differences in the number, length, type, and runtime of SVs called among them. Results Among the seven tools, Smoove and Manta both had the shortest runtime, processing files in less than 2 minutes, in contrast to tools that required more than two hours to run such as SvABA and Pindel. Smoove was the only SV caller to identify a range of SV types, while SvABA was the most restrictive, calling only breakends. All tools differed in the length of SVs called, with SvABA’s unfiltered output including the shortest length of less than 10 base pairs (bps), and Delly and BreakDancer’s output including the longest, with SVs of less than 1,000 bps. At the chromosome level, SvABA’s unfiltered output and Delly’s output included 78% and 27.5% of known SVs, respectively, with the remaining tools (including SvABA’s filtered output) achieved recall rates of less of less than 10%. By comparison, at the genomics coordinate level, no tool identified more than 20% of known SVs. Conclusions As all evaluated SV detection tools achieved poor recall rates on this comprehensive catalog of MM cell lines, this study implies SVs detected by WGS-based SV callers on WES data should be confirmed experimentally before being declared legitimate. Heterogeneity in these tools’ output lends support to their combined use in practice. Considering that many clinical grade sequencing panels continue to expand their repertoire of rearrangements with therapeutic implications, our results prompt the potential need for cancer type-matched workflows to evaluate the calling of such rearrangements.

research.abstract: Empyema necessitans is a rare complication of pleural infection in which infected pleural fluid extends through the parietal pleura into the surrounding soft tissues. We report the case of a 32-year-old man of Indian origin living in the United Kingdom who presented with worsening right-sided pleuritic chest pain, several months of night sweats, and a persistent dry cough. Five months earlier, he had been treated for right-sided pneumonia complicated by a pleural effusion, with persistent radiographic abnormalities on follow-up. Examination revealed reduced right-sided air entry and a tender, fluctuant swelling over the right posterior chest wall. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography demonstrated a posterior pleural collection extending through the chest wall into the adjacent paraspinal musculature, consistent with empyema necessitans. Ultrasound-guided aspiration yielded frank purulent fluid. Routine bacterial, anaerobic, and fungal cultures were negative. Acid-fast bacilli were not seen on initial microscopy; however, mycobacterial culture became positive after seven days, and polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing of the pleural fluid detected Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex. Whole-genome sequencing subsequently identified a lineage 1 East-African-Indian-Ocean isolate with predicted susceptibility to first-line antituberculous agents. Four-drug antituberculous therapy was commenced, with subsequent clinical and radiological improvement. This case highlights chest wall swelling as an unusual presentation of tuberculosis and emphasizes the importance of cross-sectional imaging and targeted mycobacterial testing in establishing the diagnosis.

research.abstract: Polygonatum zanlanscianense Pamp. is a perennial herb (Asparagaceae) endemic to China, whose rhizomes are used in folk medicine as a substitute for Polygonati Rhizoma. Although its plastome has been reported, the mitogenome remained uncharacterized. Here, we assembled and annotated the complete linear mitogenome of P. zanlanscianense and analysed its gene repertoire, codon usage, repeats, RNA editing sites, MTPTs, synteny, phylogeny and Ka/Ks. The 689,491-bp mitogenome (GC 46.23%) encodes 56 genes: 36 PCGs, three rRNA genes and 17 tRNA genes. Codon usage is biased toward A/U-ending codons. We identified 68 SSRs, 25 tandem repeats, 1366 dispersed repeat pairs, 585 predicted C-to-U editing sites concentrated at the first and second codon positions, and 30 MTPT fragments accounting for 2.24% of the mitogenome. Phylogenetic analysis placed P. zanlanscianense as sister to Polygonatum kingianum Collett & Hemsl. Median Ka/Ks was below 1 for 33 of the 35 genes analysed; although rpl5 and ccmB showed elevated ratios, branch-site tests did not support positive selection. This first mitogenome of P. zanlanscianense provides genomic resources for comparative genomic, phylogenetic and medicinal studies in Polygonatum.

research.abstract: Abstract Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data exhibit strong and reproducible statistical structure. This has motivated the development of large-scale foundation models, such as TranscriptFormer, that use transformer-based architectures to learn a generative model for gene expression by embedding genes into a latent vector space. These embeddings have been used to obtain state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance on downstream tasks such as cell-type classification, disease-state prediction, and cross-species learning. Here, we ask whether similar performance can be achieved without utilizing computationally intensive deep learning-based representations. Using simple, interpretable pipelines that rely on careful normalization and linear methods, we obtain SOTA or near SOTA performance across multiple benchmarks commonly used to evaluate single-cell foundation models, including outperforming foundation models on out-of-distribution tasks involving novel cell types and organisms absent from the training data. Our findings highlight the need for rigorous benchmarking and suggest that the biology of cell identity can be captured by simple linear representations of single cell gene expression data.

research.abstract: Abstract Dengue viruses 1-4 (DENV1-4) mostly circulate in endemic cycles involving humans and Aedes mosquitoes. However, rare dengue outbreaks originate from non-human primates. These spillovers are caused by sylvatic virus genotypes that are closely related to endemic strains of the same serotype, but some are caused by strains that fall between the four canonical serotypes on phylogenetic trees. It is not clear whether these genotypic differences are reflected in corresponding antigenic differences. Here, we characterized the antigenic features of QML-22, a divergent strain most closely related to DENV2. On an antigenic map, QML-22 clustered with other globally representative DENV2 strains. QML-22 was not as well neutralized by antisera raised against endemic DENV2 and was better neutralized by antisera from DENV1, 3, and 4 infections than other strains of DENV2. QML-22 had a cluster of distinct amino acid residues in domain I of the envelope (E) protein, with only scattered point mutations elsewhere in the envelope. A potently neutralizing anti-DENV2 antibody that targets this site in domain I of the E protein, 3F9, had >1000-fold lower neutralization of QML-22 than other endemic DENV2 strains, whereas other cross-reactive and DENV2-specific antibodies neutralized QML-22 and endemic strains to similar titers. When antisera from non-human primates infected with QML-22 or DENV2 reference strain S16803 were depleted with the heterologous virions, homologous neutralization was unaffected but heterologous neutralization was reduced, suggesting homologous neutralization was due to distinct epitopes. Evolutionary analyses showed the 3F9 epitope was under relaxed selection pressure compared to other neutralizing epitopes and that QML-22 had unique amino acids in this epitope relative to the likely common ancestor of all DENV2. These findings provide insight into the antigenic diversification of DENV and the possible evolution of new serotypes. Author summary Dengue viruses that are most distantly related to the four canonical serotypes originated in Borneo, suggesting this island is a possible site of early dengue virus diversification as well as continued evolution within an unidentified host species. Here, we find divergent strain QML-22 from Borneo shares many neutralizing epitopes with DENV2 but has a distinct epitope in an important region affecting potent DENV2 neutralization. This region of the virus also is variable within DENV2 and in other DENV serotypes, highlighting an important site of dengue virus diversification and evolution. The spillover threat of viruses like QML-22 remains unknown, but ecological changes in Borneo may increase this risk.

research.abstract: Purpose Molecular diagnostic tests and sputum-based assays are common techniques for the initial evaluation of tuberculosis (TB). However, given their limitations in certain clinical contexts, efforts have been made to develop other diagnostic markers. This review evaluated the diagnostic accuracy of a three-gene host-response test (TB score) for the diagnosis of TB. Methods We performed systematic searches in seven databases until July 2026. We included observational studies evaluating the diagnostic accuracy of the TB score to diagnosis of TB across different clinical contexts. Risk of bias was assessed using QUADAS-2. Meta-analysis was performed using the logit function, and GRADE was employed to assess certainty of evidence (CoE). Results Twenty-eight studies were included. For distinguishing pulmonary TB from other respiratory diseases, the TB score showed a pooled sensitivity and specificity of 0.80 (95% CI: 0.73-0.84) and 0.72 (95% CI: 0.64-0.78), respectively, with an AUC of 0.82. When comparing pulmonary TB to healthy controls, sensitivity was 0.75 and specificity was 0.86, with an AUC of 0.87. Performance was lower for meningeal tuberculosis (sensitivity 0.58; specificity 0.67) and for distinguishing active from latent TB (sensitivity 0.73; specificity 0.76). Risk of bias was generally low. The CoE for most outcomes was very low. Conclusion The TB score shows moderate diagnostic accuracy for pulmonary TB, with pooled sensitivity below the WHO TPP minimum for a standalone triage test. High heterogeneity and very low CoE limit confidence in these findings. Its potential role as a complementary tool remains investigational and requires validation in prospective studies.

research.abstract: Abstract Porcine epidemic diarrhea virus (PEDV) poses a major threat to the global swine industry. Although coronavirus discontinuous transcription is well characterized, the classical model cannot fully explain the diversity of viral RNA junctions, while conventional genome annotations may underestimate viral protein-coding capacity. To address these gaps, we integrated time-resolved RNA sequencing (RNA-seq), cycloheximide (CHX)- and harringtonine (HAR)-treated ribosome profiling (Ribo-seq), comparative genomics, and peptide mass spectrometry to investigate PEDV RNA expression and hidden coding potential. RNA-seq revealed that, at 3 hours post-infection (hpi), the 3’ genomic region exhibited strong relative coverage enrichment, whereas the relative contribution of the 5’ replicase-coding region increased rapidly between 3 and 5 hpi, suggesting a possible transition from sgRNA-dominated RNA accumulation toward enhanced genomic RNA replication. Genome-wide junction analysis identified 43,635 distinct noncanonical RNA junctions, although canonical sgRNA junctions accounted for 95.5% of all junction-supporting reads. Several abundant noncanonical sgRNAs were predicted to generate novel coding products, including N-x4, N-x2, M-x3, and M-x2, short peptides encoded within the 3’ untranslated region (UTR), and two distinct N-terminally truncated S proteins, thereby expanding the potential coding repertoire of PEDV. Genome-wide reading-frame analysis uncovered a pronounced asymmetry in hidden coding potential, identifying 68 overlapping open reading frames (ORFs) longer than 40 amino acids in the +1 reading frame, compared with only three in the +2 frame. Ribo-seq further revealed a progressive redistribution of viral ribosome occupancy toward structural protein-coding regions during the later stages of infection. By integrating HAR-associated translation initiation-site enrichment with CHX-based ORF-level translation analysis, we identified several noncanonical ORFs with strong translation-associated evidence, including N-x1, N-x2, S-x1, and ORF1b-x13. Moreover, peptide mass spectrometry detected a characteristic peptide corresponding to N-x1 in infected samples, providing independent proteomic evidence for the expression of this previously unannotated viral protein. Together, these findings uncover extensive noncanonical RNA synthesis and hidden protein-coding capacity in PEDV, establishing a foundation for understanding novel viral gene expression strategies and their potential evolutionary and pathogenic significance.

research.abstract: BACKGROUND: Species inhabiting high-elevation environments face energetic and physiological challenges, creating opportunities for adaptive divergence from lowland taxa. The yellow-tailed woolly monkey (Lagothrix flavicauda), a Critically Endangered primate endemic to high-elevation forests in Andean Perú, provides a unique system for investigating the evolutionary consequences of long-term occupation of high elevations. We used Oxford Nanopore Technology (ONT) to generate a high-coverage mitochondrial reference genome using low-quality fecal samples. Using this and a new mitogenome from a closely-related lowland common woolly monkey (L. lagotricha poeppigii), we estimated divergence dates and calculated substitution ratios to investigate the evolutionary history of both Lagothrix taxa and assess whether high-elevation living has left signatures of selection in the mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation genes of L. flavicauda. RESULTS: We assembled a high-coverage (9190X) reference mitogenome of 16,603 bp for L. flavicauda from a 15-year-old fecal sample, and a novel mitogenome for L. lagotricha poeppigii from fresh tissue (112X, 16,590 bp). Our phylogenetic reconstruction is consistent with other platyrrhine primate phylogenies with high bootstrap support, with the two Lagothrix taxa showing evidence of having diverged from one another ~ 2.8 million years ago. Substitution (d N /d S) ratios suggest purifying selection on protein-coding mitogenomic regions in all assessed lineages. CONCLUSIONS: We found no evidence of positive selection acting on mitochondrial protein-coding genes in either L. flavicauda or the broader genus Lagothrix; all analyses instead support pervasive purifying selection across genes involved in oxidative phosphorylation. These results suggest that unlike in some other non-human primates occupying high elevations, the adaptive response of L. flavicauda to living in the Andes does not appear to involve evolution in the mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation pathway, and likely involves alternative genetic pathways or mechanisms not captured by mitochondrial sequence evolution. By providing the first publicly available high-coverage mitochondrial genome for L. flavicauda, this study establishes a foundation for future population mitogenomic investigations of adaptation, evolutionary history, and conservation in this Critically Endangered, high-altitude primate.

research.abstract: BackgroundCardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) syndrome was defined in 2023 as a five-stage continuum, with stage 3 assigned on predicted rather than established cardiovascular disease. Whether that stage identifies a population whose mortality resembles clinical disease, and how health loss is distributed across stages, is unknown. MethodsWe pooled nine National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey cycles (2005-2023) and assigned CKM stages 0-4 from measured risk factors, kidney function, urine albumin, self-reported cardiovascular disease, and 10-year PREVENT risk. Years lived with disability used Global Burden of Disease weights; years of life lost combined national death counts, linked mortality files, and period life tables. ResultsIn 2021-2023, 13.8%, 21.3%, 49.1%, 6.5%, and 9.3% of adults were in stages 0 to 4, respectively. Crude mortality was 6,709 per 100,000 person-years in stage 3, comparable to 6,375 in stage 4. Adjusted hazard ratios rose from 1.39 in stage 2 to 3.22 in stage 4, with no excess in stage 1 (0.99). CKM accounted for 20.0 million DALYs annually, with 76% of attributable years of life lost in stages 3-4. Lipid-lowering therapy was absent in 53.7% of stage 3 and 33.6% of stage 4 adults, a gap unchanged over 16 years. Stage 0 prevalence fell 2.3% per year and stage 1 rose 3.1% per year between 2006 and 2016. research.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Tuberculosis contact investigation (TBCI) facilitates early detection of TB among household contacts. However, evidence on the additional contribution of repeat TBCI in high-burden settings remains limited. We assessed the contribution of repeat TBCI at 6 and 12 months to TB case detection in Kasama District, Zambia. Methods We conducted a retrospective observational cohort analysis of routinely collected programme data from five purposively selected high-volume TB diagnostic facilities. Household contacts of bacteriologically confirmed TB patients notified between January 2023 and April 2024 underwent symptom-based TB screening at baseline and at 6 and 12 months. We estimated round-specific TB detection yields, the cumulative proportion diagnosed with TB, and the contribution of repeat investigations to overall case detection. Results Among 1,250 index TB patients, 3,648 household contacts were identified and screened at baseline. TB was diagnosed in 143 (3.9%) contacts at baseline, 31 (0.9%) at month 6, and 25 (0.7%) at month 12. Overall, 199 (5.5%) contacts were diagnosed with TB across the three screening rounds, of whom 159 (79.9%) had bacteriologically confirmed disease. Repeat investigations identified 56 additional cases, representing 28.1% of all TB diagnoses. Conclusions Repeat TBCI at 6 and 12 months identified additional TB cases beyond baseline screening, although detection yields declined across successive rounds. These findings support further evaluation of risk-based follow-up strategies and more sensitive baseline screening approaches to optimize TB case detection and resource utilization in high-burden settings.

research.abstract: Abstract Background Vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus (VRE) species are common healthcare-associated pathogens that cause difficult-to-treat infections. Whole genome sequencing of patients has revealed a substantial burden of patient-to-patient VRE transmission in hospitals, with patients in intensive care units (ICUs) at particularly high risk of acquisition. However, few studies adequately characterize the pathways of VRE transmission between patients in acute care settings—a necessary step to identify current gaps in infection prevention practices. By harnessing genomic clustering analyses of whole genome sequences of VRE isolates from patients, environmental surfaces, and healthcare providers (HCP) in ICUs, we aim to reconstruct indirect pathways of pathogen movement to identify patterns of VRE spread and opportunities for transmission prevention. Methods and Findings We collected daily samples (N = 6848) from ICUs in two hospitals over 13 weeks from four main sampling sources: patients, HCP hands, patient rooms, and shared surfaces. Samples were cultured on selective media and sent for whole genome sequencing (WGS). We used genomic thresholds to identify clusters of related VRE isolates and distinguish unrelated isolates. VRE was detected in samples from 20 out of 322 unique occupant-stays (6.22%). VRE isolates were detected from all sampling sources except for shared surfaces. A total of 44 unique VRE isolates were identified, 43 Enterococcus faecium (VREfm) and one Enterococcus faecalis (VREf). Two distinct patterns of VREfm spread were observed: 1) an outbreak setting with observed patient-to-patient transmission and low VRE genomic heterogeneity, and 2) high VRE genomic heterogeneity and pathogen movement between occupant-stays facilitated by persistent HCP and environmental contamination, but no observed transmission events. VRE detection probabilities were not significantly different between occupant-stays in outbreak and non-outbreak settings (OR = 0.63, 95% CI (0.23, 1.83), p = 0.32). However, including VRE isolates from non-patient samples increased the number of occupant-stays with VRE detection from 6 to 20, a 3.3-fold increase, as compared to patient samples alone. Including non-patient samples also increased the number of VRE multi-isolate genomic clusters detected by 7-fold. Our findings are limited because sampling was primarily conducted in ICUs. Due to the combination of short ICU stay durations and imperfect test sensitivity, VRE transmission events may have been underdetected. Conclusions Our findings characterize the complex nature of VRE transmission pathways in ICU settings. Even without an ongoing outbreak, we found substantial evidence of VRE movement between occupant-stays, facilitated by a combination of HCP hands and environmental surfaces. This study highlights the importance of environmental sampling for understanding VRE transmission potential, which is likely to be underestimated using patient sampling alone. We recommend that future studies incorporate follow-up sampling after discharge to better understand the true burden of transmission.
